article_title: Effect of X-Word Grammar and Traditional Grammar Instruction on Grammatical Accuracy
citation: Sue Livingston, Andi Toce, Cyndi Casey, Fernando Montoya, Bonny R. Hart & Carmela O'Flaherty. (2018). Effect of X-Word Grammar and Traditional Grammar Instruction on Grammatical Accuracy. English Language Teaching, 11(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n3p119
title: X-Word Grammar: a construction-oriented, written-English grammar framework built on Allen's sector analysis and a small set of X-words
description: X-Word Grammar is an approach to teaching English grammar to L2 students derived from Robert L. Allen's sector analysis, which the article describes as "construction oriented, not word-oriented; and it is a grammar of written English rather than of spoken English". It organizes instruction around 20 X-words (do, have, be families and modals) that occupy the sector closest to the subject, carry all time and number meaning of the verb phrase, and dictate the form of following verbs through XV matches. Sentences are analyzed as trunks (basic subject-predicate units) that can be tested by moving the X-word to form a yes-no question, with front and end shifters and conjoined structures taught as linked patterns. The study used this framework as the experimental curriculum contrasted with a traditional structural-syllabus text.
requirements: Instruction follows practices and procedures such as those in Livingston (2010), with teachers trained in the approach
constraints: The article describes it as a grammar of written English rather than of spoken English, and lessons focus on written language
target_learners: pre-college L2 students in intensive English programs
target_learning_goals: grammatical accuracy in free written English, including tense, number agreement, verb forms and sentence patterns
examples: Experimental-group students changed New York Times sentences to yes-no questions, analyzed texts with grammar correction symbols, and did sentence manipulation activities
key_sources: Sue Livingston, Andi Toce, Cyndi Casey, Fernando Montoya, Bonny R. Hart & Carmela O'Flaherty. (2018). Effect of X-Word Grammar and Traditional Grammar Instruction on Grammatical Accuracy. English Language Teaching, 11(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n3p119

article_title: Effect of X-Word Grammar and Traditional Grammar Instruction on Grammatical Accuracy
citation: Sue Livingston, Andi Toce, Cyndi Casey, Fernando Montoya, Bonny R. Hart & Carmela O'Flaherty. (2018). Effect of X-Word Grammar and Traditional Grammar Instruction on Grammatical Accuracy. English Language Teaching, 11(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n3p119
title: X-Word Grammar lesson design: fewer unleveled forms, linked related structures, writing-focused practice with discovery techniques and narrow correction symbols
description: The article contrasts the design characteristics of X-Word Grammar lessons with traditional grammar lessons on three key issues. X-Word Grammar teaches "Substantially fewer forms that are unleveled", links related grammar forms together, focuses lessons on written language, uses "Discovery techniques including labelling of structures taught with correction symbols", bases accuracy practice on writing only, and gives feedback on narrow categories of error. Traditional grammar, by contrast, follows structural syllabi in leveled texts, disperses related forms across units, integrates lessons with spoken communicative tasks, uses pedagogic rule descriptions in a Presentation-Practice-Production sequence, and gives feedback on broad or narrow error categories.
requirements: Teachers must keep to the approach's practice activities, including cumulative use of correction symbols in practice and editing
constraints: The comparison was conducted with intermediate-level pre-college L2 students in an intensive immersion program, for about 20% of class time over three months
target_learning_goals: written grammatical accuracy and the ability to grammatically analyze English sentences
examples: In the study, the X-Word class labeled structures in authentic readings with correction symbols and analyzed supplemental texts, while the traditional class used workbook activities such as fill-in-the-blank and completing conversations
